title: Real-Time Sign Language to Text Conversion Using Mediapipe Hand Landmarks and Random Forest Classifier
authors: S. H; S. M; Syed Irfan M; Thurai Pandian M
venue: International Conference Trends Material Science and Inventive Materials
abstract: This paper introduces a live sign language translation converter from gesture to text using hand landmark detection and classical machine learning. In brief, our method utilizes MediaPipe Hands to obtain 21 normalized hand landmark points from webcam video, which are then represented as a low, dimensional geometric feature vector. This vector serves as input to a Random Forest classification algorithm to identify isolated static sign language gestures representing alphabets and numbers. Compared to other methods based on deep learning that have high computational demand, our system is lightweight, interpretable, and capable of running in real time on regular CPU hardware only. Based on the experimental results, the system achieves an overall recognition accuracy of about 98.9 percent, and the performance is quite consistent between different gesture classes. Additionally, the system without GPU acceleration runs at a speed of 20, 30 frames per second and can be therefore considered an attending tool for people with disabilities in ac- cessibility, education, and human, computer interaction domains.

title: Real-Time Sign Language Recognition and Speech Synthesis Browser Extension
authors: R. Murugesan; K. V.; S. B; Santhosh S. S.; Bhavesh Kumaran J. U; G. P
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Sign language is the primary mode of communication for deaf and mute individuals. However, communication between sign language users and non-signers remains a major challenge. This project proposes a real-time sign language recognition system that converts hand gestures into text and speech using a browser extension. The system utilises computer vision and deep learning techniques to recognise hand gestures through a live camera feed. MediaPipe is used for hand landmark detection, and a trained classification model converts gestures into textual output. The generated text is displayed as subtitles within the browser extension and further converted into speech using a text-to-speech engine. This solution enables seamless communication in real-time environments such as online meetings, classrooms, and public services. The proposed system is lightweight, accessible, and deployable as a browser extension, making it practical for everyday use.

title: Real-Time Sign Language Recognition Using Hand Landmarks with Adaptive Retraining Mechanism
authors: C. A; S. S; M. M; H. M; S. K; K. S.
venue: 2026 Fourth International Conference on Augmented Intelligence and Sustainable Systems (ICAISS)
abstract: Sign language is the main form of communication among the hearing and speech impaired individuals, but interacting with non-signers is still a challenge. To overcome this weakness, this paper introduces a sign language recognition system in real-time and is founded on computer vision and deep learning methods. A standard webcam is used to record hand gestures and MediaPipe framework is used to extract discriminative hand landmarks. These landmark features are then categorized into the respective alphabetic signs through the use of a trained supervised deep learning model with a custom generated dataset.The proposed system does not require any external sensors to work and instead uses only visionbased inputs, hence making it cost-effective and easy to deploy. To improve the user-friendliness, a dual-screen interface is added with one display showing the live video feed along with the identified hand landmarks, and the other display showing the identified alphabet in real-time. Moreover, sequential letter accumulation mechanism is introduced to provide the opportunity to create words dynamically in order to enhance extensive practicality of communication. Through experimental testing, it is proven that real-time performance was reliable and gesture recognition successful under different conditions. The presented framework indicates the possibility of landmark-based sign language interpretation and presents a scaling approach to assistive communication and educational tools as well as humancomputer interaction applications.

title: Real-Time Sign Language Recognition System using Computer Vision and Deep Learning
authors: S. Shelke; Sanskruti C. Shrirang; Pratham C. Durge; Lande M. V.; Akshay B. Nagde
venue: International Scientific Journal of Engineering and Management
abstract: Sign language serves as a communication method for individuals who are deaf or mute. Despite this, there are still communication challenges between those with hearing impairments and those without, primarily due to the absence of automated interpretation systems. This project introduces a real-time sign language recognition system that leverages computer vision and machine learning. The system utilizes alive camera feed to capture hand gestures, identifies hand landmarks with Media Pipe, and emp loys a trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model to classifythese gestures. The identified gestures are then translated into text, with suggestions for commonly used wordsprovided to enhance communicat ion efficiency. The system is designed to be user-friendly, affordable, and capable of operating in real time without the need for specialized hardware, thus aiding in closing the communication gap and fostering inclusivity.Key Words:Sign Language Recognition, Hand Gesture Recognition,Machine Learning, Deep Learning, CNN, Computer Vision,Media Pipe

title: Real-Time Sign Language Recognition Framework Utilizing 3D Pose Estimation and Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: I. P. Kumar; K. R. Reddy; G. S. Kumar; N. Rajasekhar; Nallabothula Vinod Kumar; Famida Begum
venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Computer Science Engineering and Information Technology
abstract: Sign language serves as the primary mode of communication for the hearing and speech-impaired community. However, a significant communication gap exists between sign language users and non-signers, necessitating the development of automated translation systems. This paper presents a robust Sign Language Recognition (SLR) system designed to interpret isolated gestures from video sequences. The proposed methodology leverages Google MediaPipe for efficient, lightweight 3D pose extraction, capturing spatial dependencies of hand and body keypoints. These temporal sequences are subsequently processed using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to classify gestures. Experimental results utilizing a subset of the WLASL dataset demonstrate that the proposed skeleton-based approach achieves high recognition accuracy while maintaining low computational complexity, making it suitable for deployment in real-time accessibility applications.

title: Real-Time Sign Language Detection using MediaPipe Hand Landmarks and LSTM Networks
authors: Abin Roy; Alok Ajith Suja; P. S.; A. K.
venue: 2026 4th International Conference on Intelligent Cyber Physical Systems and Internet of Things (ICoICI)
abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) is vital for addressing the communication barrier between hearing-impaired people and the rest of the population. This paper presents a real-time SLR system employing hand landmark extraction in a vision-based system and time-dependent deep learning. This involves MediaPipe to extract three-dimensional hand keypoints from live video streams and a Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) network to learn temporal dependencies of dynamic sign gestures. The system was trained and evaluated using a dataset of six gestures that are commonly used: ‘Hello’, ‘Thank You’, ‘Yes’, ‘No’, ‘Namaste’, and ‘Welcome’. Every gesture was coded as a series of 30 frames with 126 features of landmarks on the hand in each frame. It has been shown experimentally that the proposed system attains a classification rate of 91.67%, high class-wise precision and recall rates for all gestures analyzed. Multi-class Receiver Operating Characteristic analysis also affirms a high degree of class separability with Area Under the Curve (AUC) values of up to 1.00. The findings show that the proposed method can capture the spatial and temporal gesture features effectively with low computational complexity; thus, it can be used in real time recognition systems of sign language.

title: Real-Time Sign Language Chat Application with Speech Output
authors: Bidish Kumar Nayak; Bibhuti Kumar Giri; Saudamini Samantaray
venue: American Journal of AI Digital Transformation and Regenerative Pharmacist
matched_terms: sign language recognition, sign language translation, landmark
abstract: The proliferation of digital communication technologies has dramatically transformed human interaction, yet individuals with hearing and speech impairments continue to face significant barriers in mainstream communication systems. Sign language remains the primary mode of communication for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community; however, the vast majority of people outside this community are unable to comprehend it. This communication gap necessitates the development of intelligent, technology-driven bridge systems that can translate sign language into readable and audible formats in real time. Traditional solutions such as human interpreters are expensive, logistically complex, and unavailable in many situations. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, computer vision, and real-time web technologies have opened new possibilities for automated sign language translation. Technologies such as Google’s MediaPipe hand landmark detection framework, WebSocketbased real-time communication, and neural text-to-speech synthesis have matured to the point where accurate, low-latency sign language recognition and translation is practically achievable in browser-based applications. However, many existing automated translation systems suffer from critical limitations: they require specialized, expensive hardware such as data gloves or motion capture suits, are designed as standalone offline applications rather than integrated communication platforms, support only a limited vocabulary, and lack real-time performance necessary for fluid conversation. This project presents the design and implementation of a RealTime Sign Language Chat Application with Speech Output—a full-stack AI-powered system that enables seamless communication using hand gesture recognition. The gesture recognition engine is built using MediaPipe’s hand landmark detection framework, which tracks 21 key points on the human hand in real time through a webcam feed. A rule-based classifier processes the geometric relationships between these landmarks to accurately identify 55 distinct gesture categories: 26 American Sign Language (ASL) alphabetic letters, 10 numeric gestures, and 19 special phrase gestures including greetings, expressions, and commonly used functional words.

title: Real-Time Phrase-Level Sign Language Recognition Using Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Region Proposal and GCN-Based Sequence Consensus
authors: S. Athinarayanan; B.Manindra Sai; Y.Nikhitha
venue: 2026 1st International Conference on Innovation & Growth in Next-Gen Intelligent Technology & Engineering (IGNITE)
abstract: Meaningful communication with the approximately 360 million people worldwide affected by disabling hearing loss remains a significant hurdle in human-computer interaction. While previous vision-based Sign Language Recognition (SLR) systems have made strides, they often rely on rigid, pixel-heavy architectures that struggle under the weight of real-world environmental noise, such as shifting illumination or cluttered backgrounds. In this paper, we propose a reformulated framework designed for the complexities of phrase-level recognition. Our approach centres on the Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Region Proposal (A-STRAP) algorithm for robust skeletal landmark normalisation, paired with a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) that treats the human skeleton as a dynamic, non-Euclidean graph. By integrating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layers with a novel Phrase-Level Sequence Consensus (PL-SC) mechanism, we achieve a high degree of stability across variable-length gesture sequences. Experimental validation across standard benchmarks (WLASL, AUTSL) and conversational datasets confirms a peak accuracy of 95.1% at 45 frames per second (FPS), outperforming standard CNN-LSTM baselines with high statistical significance(p < 0.001) over standard CNN-LSTM baselines.

title: Real-Time Multi-Sign Language Recognition and Translation
authors: Tabasum Guledgudd; Mr. Siddarth Hugar; Ms. Rakshita V; Ms. Soumya patil; Ms. Sushmita A; Ms. A. Usha
venue: Engineering and Technology Journal
abstract: Sign language constitutes the primary mode of communication for an estimated 466 million deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals worldwide, yet the overwhelming majority of hearing individuals cannot understand it. Existing sign language recognition and translation systems address only a single sign language in isolation, are limited to static gestures or a small lexicon, lack real-time bidirectional translation, and fail to support multiple regional sign languages simultaneously. This paper proposes UnifySign: a unified, AI-powered, real-time framework for multi-sign language recognition and translation, supporting Indian Sign Language (ISL), American Sign Language (ASL), Pakistan Sign Language (PSL), and Indo-Pakistani Sign Language (IPSL). The system integrates YOLOv8 for bounding-box detection, MediaPipe Holistic for 21-point hand landmark extraction, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for static sign classification, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for dynamic gesture sequence recognition, and a Large Language Model (Google Flan-T5) for grammatically coherent sentence generation. A bidirectional translation pipeline supports both sign-to-text and speech/text-to-sign directions. Offline mobile deployment (Flutter + TFLite) and a web-based interface (Flask) ensure accessibility across device types. Experimental evaluation on INCLUDE, MS-ASL, WLASL, and a custom PSL/IPSL corpus demonstrates accuracy exceeding 97% for ISL/ASL static recognition, 95% for dynamic gestures, and 91% for sentence-level translation. The proposed system surpasses all ten reviewed state-of-the-art systems in coverage, accuracy, and real-world deployability.

title: Real-Time Indian Sign Language Recognition and Speech Translation with Analytics Using MediaPipe and LSTM
authors: B. Mohanraj; G. M; M. Vasantha Priya; S. S; J. R.; Soumya George
venue: 2026 International Conference on Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision (ICNPCV)
abstract: Communication difficulties between Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHH) and the hearing world persist and hinder effective communication in education, healthcare, workplaces, and public services. With the recent developments in computer vision and deep learning, automated sign language recognition has been possible; however, most of the existing sign language recognition systems mainly concentrate on gesture classification and provide less support to real-time speech translation and performance monitoring. In this paper, a realtime Indian Sign Language (ISL) recognition and speech translation system using MediaPipe Holistic and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks is proposed. The system uses common RGB camera to capture hand gestures, and uses MediaPipe Holistic to extract hand landmark features to get a rich representation of hand movements and minimize the effect of background and lighting changes. Temporal gesture pattern modeling is done by an LSTM network to accurately recognize the dynamic ISL gestures. The known signs are then translated into text and then into speech, allowing the easy exchange of information between signers and non-signers. An integrated analytics module is designed to capture and analyse recognition events to support system evaluation and user interaction analysis. This is validated experimentally with the benchmark INCLUDE-50 dataset that consists of 50 isolated ISL word classes. The developed system achieved an accuracy of 96.42%, precision of 95.87%, recall of 95.31%, and an F1-score of 95.59%. In addition, it achieved a Cohen's Kappa coefficient of 0.947 and an MCC of 0.942 with an average inference time of 28.4 ms, end-to-end latency of 82 ms, processing speed of 30.1 FPS and memory usage of 412 MB. The outcomes illustrate the feasibility of the proposed system in terms of accuracy, computation efficiency and applicability for real-time assistive communication applications.

title: Real-Time Indian Sign Language Recognition Using Hand Landmarks and ANN with Hindi Speech Output
authors: Deepanshi; Geetanjali Sharma; Nishika Raj; Sharmila; Priyanka Tyagi; Kashika Singh
venue: 2026 IEEE 6th International Conference on Computing, Power, and Communication Technologies (IC2PCT)
abstract: This proposed work aims to narrow the gap between those who know Indian Sign Language (ISL) and those who do not know it. The authors have introduced an AI-based system that can convert ISL gestures into Hindi text and speech. The idea is to recognize hand movements using a webcam and convert the action into text and speech in real-time. The system has used MediaPipe to recognize 21 landmarks on the hand and combine them into a 63-dimensional vector. After normalizing this vector, it has used an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) to classify the gestures into words. The data includes various ISL gesture classes under different lighting conditions to increase robustness. For converting text into speech, Google Text-toSpeech (gTTS), is used to converts the text into spoken language in real-time. The system has used TensorFlow and OpenCV to implement this system. The experimental results show an accuracy of around $94-95 {\%}$, and it has low latency, and suitable for real-time usage with typical hardware and webcam. The idea is to make ISL more accessible and communicative by converting it into Hindi text and speech.

title: Real-Time Hand Gesture Recognition Using HOG-SVM: A Computationally Efficient Approach for Assistive Technologies
authors: R. Kagalkar; Gurusiddappa Hugar
venue: Sakarya University Journal of Computer and Information Sciences
abstract: This research proposes a real-time hand gesture recognition system for assistive technology, mainly for sign language translation. This system is meant to achieve maximum computational efficiency for real-time applications on resource-constrained devices. Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) feature extraction and Support Vector Machine (SVM) are utilized by the proposed method for the task of gesture recognition. Since it can extract both edge-based and shape-based features of the gesture, this method can be used for the detection of dynamic and static gestures. This system relies on the pre-processed set of varying gestures presented in the Word-Level American Sign Language (WLASL) dataset, which is readily accessible, to be effective in varying circumstances of illumination, backgrounds and hand pose. Pre-processing techniques such as grayscale conversion, noise removal and frame resizing were used for feature extraction, helping in the improvement of feature extraction at a very low computation cost. HOG features that possess useful gesture boundaries and shape were extracted from the pre-processed frames. Features were then classified by SVM with the help of an RBF kernel. SVM classifier with the RBF kernel has an efficiency in recognizing the gestures at the variation of non-linear shapes with an accuracy of 97.8%. This system’s performance can be increased using the hybrid features by using HOG and Local Binary Patterns (LBP) together. Furthermore, HMMs are used to model the temporal dependencies for smooth recognition of dynamic gestures while applying data augmentation techniques like rotation, scaling, and flipping to maximize the generalization and adaptability of the model. The proposed system was compared with deep learning models such as CNNs, ResNet, and MobileNet. Although deep learning models achieved slightly higher accuracy, they required significantly higher computational resources. The proposed HOG-SVM model achieved a better trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency for real-time applications. This study demonstrates the model’s potential to integrate into sign language translation systems, smart assistive devices, and gesture-controlled interfaces as a practical solution for improving human-computer interaction.

title: Real-Time Gesture-to-Text Translation for American Sign Language Using MediaPipe and LSTM
authors: Younesse Ouahbi; Ilham Mdarhri; Nouhaila Nseri; Noha Benlkahla; Najlae Zaroual; Soraya Mellaj; S. Ziti
venue: European Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: For millions of deaf and hard-of-hearing people around the world, sign language serves as their primary form of communication. However, the hearing population’s limited comprehension of sign language means that communication barriers still exist. Even though sign language recognition research has advanced significantly in recent years, many current methods only use isolated signs or heavily annotated datasets and computationally demanding models, which restricts their use in real-time and resource-constrained settings. This paper presents a vision-based lightweight framework for phrase-level American Sign Language (ASL) recognition from video sequences. In order to capture the dynamic evolution of hand gestures, the suggested method uses MediaPipe for hand skeletal landmark extraction and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for temporal modeling. The system preserves the necessary motion information for precise recognition while reducing visual complexity by representing gestures as series of hand landmarks. Robustness to signer variability, environmental changes, and dynamic gesture transitions are key components of the methodological design, which is based on a review of recent literature. The suggested framework is appropriate for real-time assistive communication and human–computer interaction applications since landmark-based temporal modeling provides a good trade-off between recognition accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Real-Time Dual-Language Sign Language Recognition Using a Hybrid DNN-LSTM Architecture with Motion-Based Model Switching
authors: P. E. Rubini; Karri Pujitha; Shashank. M; Shreyas S. Rao
venue: 2026 2nd International Conference on Intelligent Systems and Computational Networks (ICISCN)
matched_terms: sign language recognition, sign language translation, landmark
abstract: Sign language recognition systems play a critical role in enabling communication between hearing-impaired individuals and the general population. Although deep learningbased solutions have improved gesture classification accuracy, most existing systems focus on either static alphabet recognition or dynamic word recognition independently. Furthermore, multilingual support remains limited, particularly for Indian Sign Language (ISL). This paper presents a real-time duallanguage sign language recognition framework supporting both American Sign Lan-guage (ASL) and ISL. The proposed system integrates Medi-aPipe-based landmark extraction with a hybrid deep learning architecture consisting of Deep neural network (DNN) models for static alphabet recognition based on landmark features and LSTM models for dynamic word-level recognition. A motion-driven state controller automatically switches between static and dynamic recognition pipelines, eliminating inference conflicts. Experimental results demonstrate high classification accuracy for alphabet recognition and robust performance for dynamic gesture recognition under real-time constraints. The architecture is scalable, modular, and suitable for practical deployment. The proposed system introduces a motion-driven state controller for automatic switching between static and dynamic gesture recognition. The framework supports dual-language recognition (ASL and ISL) in real time, providing a scalable and efficient solution for sign language translation.

title: Real-Time Continuous Sign Language Translation System
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
abstract: Due to the general public's ignorance of sign language, communication between hearing-impaired people and the general public continues to be extremely difficult. Current systems are primarily concerned with recognizing static gestures; they are unable to comprehend continuous dynamic gestures that are used in actual communication. In this paper, a real-time continuous sign language translation system utilizing deep learning and computer vision techniques is proposed. The system uses a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to capture temporal dependencies and MediaPipe to extract hand landmark key-points. Real-time processing of gesture sequences results in meaningful text output. To enable efficient communication, the generated text is further converted into audible speech. In contrast to image-based techniques, a vector-based strategy is employed to lower computational complexity.

title: Real-Time Adaptive Hand Gesture Recognition using Hybrid Random Forest and LSTM Models
authors: Karthik; Parshini B. K.; Pavitra J. Poojary; Prarthana S. Bhangera; Sannidhi S. Shetty
venue: 2026 4th International Conference on Intelligent Cyber Physical Systems and Internet of Things (ICoICI)
abstract: Sign Language Recognition is a crucial application in the field of communication for the deaf & mute people. This work introduces a real-time vision-based hand gesture recognition system to implement sign-to-text and sign-to-speech communication via computer vision and machine learning techniques. The proposed framework involves extracting hand landmarks from images using MediaPipe and using a hybrid classification method that includes a Random Forest (RF) static gesture classification model and an LSTM dynamic gesture classification model. The routing mechanism is based on a motion detection mechanism that automatically switches from the static to dynamic recognition mode to enhance real-time performance. An adaptive learning module is included, which adapts gesture recognition to user-specific hand patterns. The recognized gestures are translated into text and speech by an embedded speech-to-text application. The experimental results showed that in the static gesture, the accuracy was 99.47%, and in the dynamic gesture, the accuracy was 91.2% for real-time gesture recognition. The suggested system is very low-cost and contactless and is adaptive for assisting communication in a practical deployment system.

title: Real Time Sign Language Translation on Raspberry PI Using Lightweight Neural Networks
authors: Ravi Bolimera; S. Gudepu; S. R. Devi; V. Kumar; K. Thirumalamma
venue: 2026 IEEE Global Symposium on Emerging and Communication Technologies (GSEACT)
abstract: This paper presents a real time ASL fingerspelling recognizer system which is based on hand based landmark based LSTM network driven recognizer. It is easily scalable to low cost hardware, which has low latency output, and has an advantage in real time assistive applications, which are light weight in property. A further direction of the work is to evolve the system at the direction of constant sign recognition, bi manual signatures, and facial expression as well as making the more of the models accurate and robust.

title: Real Time Sign Language Recognition with Text to Speech Integration
authors: Shalini Joseph; Hansika Yeddula; L. Gyan Rao Nazre; Madhumitha R. Aithal
venue: 2026 4th International Conference on Knowledge Engineering and Communication Systems (ICKECS)
abstract: One of the most important forms of communication for people with speech or hearing problems is sign language; however, its limited understanding among non signers often restricts effective interaction. This paper presents a real time Indian Sign Language (ISL) recognition system integrated with Text to Speech (TTS) conversion to address this challenge. The proposed system employs MediaPipe for accurate hand landmark detection and extracts 3D spatial coordinates as gesture features. These features are classified using optimized machine learning models, including Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Random Forest. To improve classification performance and mitigate data imbalance, the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) is applied during training. Communication is made simple and accessible by translating the identified motions into speech and text. Experimental findings show that the system attains a high level of accuracy, real time responsiveness, and robust performance under varying conditions. The proposed approach highlights the effectiveness of integrating gesture recognition with speech synthesis as a scalable assistive technology for inclusive human computer interaction.

title: Real Time Sign Language Recognition and Translation to Text for Vocally and Hearing-Impaired People
authors: Mohammed Saqeeb; Jonah Joseph Yama; Mohammad Ali Mulla; Mahammad Ayan hebballi
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Applied Science
abstract: The Real-Time Sign Language Recognition and Translation system shown in this study aims to improve communication between sign language users and non-sign language speakers. The system uses a webcam to record hand movements, which are then processed using OpenCV for real-time image processing and MediaPipe for hand landmark identification. Next, American Sign Language (ASL) movements are accurately classified using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Smoother and more natural communication is made possible by a Text-to-Speech (TTS) engine that translates the identified motions into readable text and then into speech.

title: RECOGNIZING AND UNDERSTANDING AMERICAN SIGN LANGUAGE USING DEEP LEARNING AND MEDIAPIPE
authors: Anh Tu Nguyen; Luong Thai Le; Hiếu Trung Trần; Huong Thi Diem Nguyen; M. Nguyen
venue: Journal of Science Natural Science
abstract: Sign language serves as the primary medium of expression serves as the primary medium of expression for deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals. However, interpersonal interaction remains challenging, as they primarily rely on sign language to express their thoughts. To address this issue, this study proposes an automated sign language recognition and interpretation framework, integrating static and dynamic recognition components. Specifically, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is employed for static gesture classification, while a hybrid CNN- Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) architecture is utilized to capture the spatiotemporal features of dynamic signs. Furthermore, MediaPipe is leveraged for robust landmark localization to enhance feature extraction. The American Sign Language (ASL) dataset used in this research ensures diversity in sign representation, including variations in hand shapes, positions, and movements. The proposed models achieved high accuracy, with the CNN model reaching 93.1% and the CNN-LSTM model achieving 94.1% on test datasets, confirming their effectiveness in ASL recognition tasks.

title: REAL TIME SIGN LANGUAGE TRANSLATION AND AUDIO TRANSLATION ON VIDEO CALLS
authors: Prajwal Bhosale, Dhruv Bendre, Sandhya Tiwari and Rohini Bhosale
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
matched_terms: sign language recognition, sign language translation, landmark
abstract: Communication barriers continue to affect individuals with speech impairments who rely on sign language, especially during real-time digital communication such as video calls. Most current video conferencing platforms do not support built-in sign language interpretation, which forces users to depend on text chat or third-party assistance. This paper presents a multi-modal WebRTC-based framework designed to enable realtime sign language recognition, text translation, and cross-language audio generation during live video communication. The proposed system works as an intelligent processing layer that runs alongside the video stream, allowing smooth and natural interaction without delay. Instead of analyzing full image frames, the system extracts threedimensional hand landmark coordinates using MediaPipe and CVZone. These coordinates are processed using NumPy arrays, allowing the model to focus on gesture structure rather than background details such as lighting or environment noise. This coordinate-based approach improves recognition reliability while maintaining fast processing speed, making the system suitable for low-bandwidth video calls. During communication, recognized hand gestures are instantly converted into text and further synthesized into speech, allowing hearing participants to listen to the sign language as spoken audio. At the same time, spoken communication from the other participant is converted into text and displayed for the signer. By combining sign-to-speech and speech-to-text capabilities, the framework creates a two-way accessible communication environment. The results demonstrate that the system provides stable real-time performance with reliable recognition accuracy during live video calls, highlighting its potential to improve digital accessibility and support inclusive communication. Keywords: Sign Language Recognition, WebRTC, Multi-Modal Systems, Real-Time Translation, Accessibility, Audio Synthesis

title: RAIDAL: Redundancy-Aware Information Density Active Learning for CTC-Based Continuous Sign Language Recognition
authors: Rafael A. Diniz Augusto; Gabriel L. Oliveira; Erickson R. Nascimento
venue: arXiv preprint
abstract: Continuous sign language recognition (CSLR) is a key technology for accessibility, yet its development remains limited by the high cost of annotating continuous video streams. Active learning offers a path toward mitigating this cost, but standard acquisition functions are not designed for weakly aligned sign language videos, where sign executions are interleaved with rest poses, irregular pauses, sign-like motion, and temporally redundant frames. This temporal redundancy can undermine sample selection, as acquisition scores may be influenced by timesteps from regions that are not associated with the decoded gloss sequence, distorting the video's estimated informativeness. In this work, we show that modern CSLR models already contain a mechanism for identifying gloss-level temporal evidence: the CTC decoder. Although typically used only during inference, its alignment peaks indicate where the model localizes each predicted gloss in the feature sequence, providing a source of temporal structure for active learning acquisition functions at zero additional labeling cost. Thus, we introduce RAIDAL (Redundancy-Aware Information Density Active Learning), which repurposes the CTC decoder to restrict representation-based scoring to decoder-aligned gloss regions, rather than exposing the acquisition function to the entire unfiltered video. Across three datasets and two architectures, RAIDAL achieves its strongest data-efficiency gains over competing baselines in large-vocabulary, budget-limited settings, while remaining competitive in the smaller-vocabulary, large-budget setting. The code used in this work is publicly available at github.com/verlab/RAIDAL.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Spatio-Temporal Deep Learning Framework for Real-Time Sign Language Translation
authors: Suriya Durai Murugan T; K. M.; M. Ramnath
venue: International Journal of Science, Strategic Management and Technology
abstract: Real-time sign language translation remains a significant challenge in assistive technology due to the complexity of capturing dynamic hand gestures and interpreting them accurately. This paper presents a Hybrid Quantum CNN-LSTM based Real-Time Sign Language Translation System, designed to bridge the communication gap between hearing-impaired individuals and the general population. The system integrates computer vision, deep learning, and quantum machine learning, where live video input is captured using OpenCV and hand landmarks are extracted using MediaPipe to obtain 42 three-dimensional joint coordinates. These landmarks are processed as temporal sequences and passed through a hybrid architecture combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for spatial feature extraction, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) for temporal modeling, and a Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) layer implemented using PennyLane to capture complex non-linear relationships through quantum embedding and entanglement. Unlike traditional deep learning models, the proposed system employs a parallel quantum-classical framework that enhances feature representation while maintaining computational efficiency. The model is trained using augmented datasets with techniques such as temporal expansion, geometric transformations, and noise injection to improve robustness and generalization. Experimental results demonstrate an F1-score of approximately 0.93, achieving competitive performance with reduced parameter complexity and enabling real-time translation on standard computing devices. This work highlights the potential of hybrid quantum-classical models in real-time computer vision applications and provides an efficient, scalable solution for assistive communication technologies

title: Quality-Aware Adaptive Fusion for Degradation-Robust Continuous Sign Language Recognition
authors: Chuang Guo; Lixuan Zhao; Min Li; Han Ren; Mingshuo Sun; Bao-Long Zhu
venue: 2026 8th International Conference on Electronic Engineering and Informatics (EEI)
abstract: Continuous sign language recognition (CSLR) transcribes sign language sentences from unsegmented video. Real-world video quality is often degraded by low resolution, high lighting, noise, motion blur, and lossy compression, which degrade RGB-based recognition accuracy. We propose QAAF-CSLR, a dual-modal framework leveraging RGB appearance and skeleton keypoint geometry. A Degradation-Asymmetric Training (DAT) strategy randomly degrades only RGB frames while keeping skeleton sequences intact, and a Quality-Aware Adaptive Fusion (QAAF) module dynamically adjusts bimodal fusion weights based on inferred input quality. We construct CE-CNSL-D, a degradation benchmark with 16 test conditions. Experiments show consistent gains under clean and degraded inputs, with DAT providing the largest robustness improvements and QAAF yielding consistent fusion refinements across all conditions. Scope: clean-frame pose estimation can be optimistic for end-to-end noisy capture; we discuss applicability and future robust-pose directions in Sec. III-C.

title: QUALITY-AWARE POSE–HAND KEYPOINT EXTRACTION PIPELINE FOR SKELETON-BASED SIGN LANGUAGE RECOGNITION
authors: D. Akbarov; T. Sembayev; A. Kydyrbekova
venue: NEWS of National Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Kazakhstan
abstract: Skeleton-based sign language recognition (SLR) uses pose and hand keypoints as a compact, background-invariant representation, but in real signing videos the keypoint stream produced by off-the-shelf estimators is often unreliable. Hand trajectories frequently contain missing detections, left/right identity swaps, duplicate outputs, temporal jitter, and occlusion-related drift. These artifacts are not merely preprocessing noise: they directly degrade the quality of downstream SLR training. This paper presents a quality-aware pose–hand keypoint extraction pipeline that treats keypoint generation as an auditable, reliability-aware stage rather than a hidden preprocessing step. The proposed method combines: (i) pose-guided left/right hand assignment with spatial gating, (ii) pose-conditioned second-pass region-of-interest (ROI) refinement for low-confidence or missing hands, (iii) lightweight short-gap temporal bridging (tracking/hold), (iv) explicit occlusion-consistent labeling, (v) plausibility checks to reject physically implausible configurations, and (vi) anchor-preserving postprocessing for short-gap filling and jitter reduction. Beyond cleaned keypoints, the pipeline exports per-hand reliability semantics (provenance and state) and a dataset-ready quality report based on proxy metrics, including coverage, confidence, recovery fractions, intervention rates, and temporal stability indicators. A fixed composite quality score is also defined to support reproducible ranking and filtering without manually annotated hand landmarks. Dataset-scale evaluation on Slovo (n = 20,400 clips) shows that the proposed full configuration substantially improves extraction reliability over a pass1-only baseline: the composite quality score increases from 0.684 to 0.794, any-hand coverage from 0.889 to 0.969, and both-hands coverage from 0.454 to 0.646, while MissingRate decreases from 0.329 to 0.193. Recovery analysis further shows that most robustness gains come from ROI-based second-pass recovery, with tracking acting mainly as a sparse fallback mechanism. The pipeline is designed for reproducible keypoint export, dataset curation, and reliability-aware SLR training.

title: Pose-based Contrastive Representation Learning for Sign Languages
authors: Ushnish Sarkar; Bhaswar Chattopadhyay; Tapas Samanta; H.K Pandey; N.P. Yalagoud
venue: 2026 International Conference on Computing, Electronics & Communications Engineering (ICCECE)
abstract: Abstract Sign language processing remains challenging due to the scarcity of large, well-annotated datasets and the strong linguistic specificity of sign languages across regions. Most existing sign language recognition and translation systems rely on gloss or text supervision, limiting their applicability to low-resource sign languages where such annotations are unavailable. In this work, we propose a pose-based contrastive representation-learning framework that learns sign language representations purely from articulatory structure, without relying on text or gloss labels. Each sign video is represented as a sequence of pose landmarks extracted using MediaPipe and encoded using a Transformer-based temporal model trained with a supervised contrastive objective. The model is trained on the ASL Citizen dataset and evaluated in a zero-shot cross-lingual retrieval setting on the INCLUDE and LSA64 datasets, representing Indian and Argentinian Sign Languages respectively. Experimental results demonstrate strong embedding discrimination in pairwise evaluation and high zero-shot retrieval performance, achieving Recall @1 of 97.12 percent on LSA64 and 88.6 percent on INCLUDE, with Recall@5 and Recall@10 exceeding 96 percent on both datasets. These results indicate that articulatory pose information alone is sufficient to learn robust and transferable sign representations across languages. The proposed approach offers a scalable alternative for sign language understanding in under-resourced settings and provides a foundation for cross-lingual retrieval and similarity-based sign learning applications.

title: Pose-Based Static Sign Language Recognition with Deep Learning for Turkish, Arabic, and American Sign Languages
authors: Rıdvan Yayla; Hakan Ucgun; Mahmud Abbas
venue: Italian National Conference on Sensors
abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence have significantly enhanced communication for individuals with hearing impairments. This study presents a robust cross-lingual Sign Language Recognition (SLR) framework for Turkish, American English, and Arabic sign languages. The system utilizes the lightweight MediaPipe library for efficient hand landmark extraction, ensuring stable and consistent feature representation across diverse linguistic contexts. Datasets were meticulously constructed from nine public-domain sources (four Arabic, three American, and two Turkish). The final training data comprises curated image datasets, with frames for each language carefully selected from varying angles and distances to ensure high diversity. A comprehensive comparative evaluation was conducted across three state-of-the-art deep learning architectures—ConvNeXt (CNN-based), Swin Transformer (ViT-based), and Vision Mamba (SSM-based)—all applied to identical feature sets. The evaluation demonstrates the superior performance of contemporary vision Transformers and state space models in capturing subtle spatial cues across diverse sign languages. Our approach provides a comparative analysis of model generalization capabilities across three distinct sign languages, offering valuable insights for model selection in pose-based SLR systems.

title: PoET: Lightweight Pose Encoder Transformer for Online Sign Language Recognition
authors: Julie Lascar; Jules Françoise; Michèle Gouiffès; Annelies Braffort; Diandra Fabre
venue: International Conference on Computer Vision Theory and Applications
abstract: : With the growing demand for accessible technological tools in the field of sign language (SL) processing, numerous recognition models have been developed in recent years. This paper presents a pose-based lightweight Transformer encoder designed for real-time isolated sign recognition. We provide a detailed description of the model’s architecture, together with a dedicated preprocessing pipeline. We present a comprehensive evaluation of our approach on widely used video datasets, including WLASL, AUTSL, ASL Citizen, which encompass diverse environments, multiple scales, and different SL. Our approach matches or even surpasses recent state-of-the-art methods, requiring fewer parameters, less memory, and lower computational cost. Additionally, we conduct an experiment via an online web platform, with deaf users. This experiment assesses the performance of our model in a real-world context where conditions differ between training and inference. This paper highlights the strong potential of lightweight pose-based architectures for practical SL recognition systems and provides concrete technical guidance for effective implementation.

title: Phonological Perception of Sign Language Models
authors: Kayo Yin; Jessica Carter; Alex Xijie Lu; Annemarie Kocab
venue: arXiv preprint
abstract: Sign languages are compositional systems where meaning arises by combining sublexical phonological parameters, such as handshape, location, and movement. While deep learning models for Sign Language Recognition (SLR) have achieved increased performance on translation benchmarks, it remains unclear whether these models distinguish abstract phonological features or merely rely on low-level statistical correlations. This work evaluates the phonological perception of SLR models trained on American Sign Language (ASL) by probing phonological sensitivity using minimal pairs and evaluating representational alignment with human behavioral data. Our results reveal that SLR models exhibit emergent phonological sensitivity, but with clear architectural trade-offs: pose-based models are sensitive to handshape contrasts, while pixel-based models better capture location changes. Furthermore, pose-based models learn latent representations that correlate with human perceptual similarity judgments (r~0.49). These findings suggest that while SLR models exhibit emergent phonology, current training paradigms are insufficient to scale them beyond their architectural inductive biases.

title: Optimized Emergency Sign Language Recognition with Large-Kernel Attention Graph Convolutional Network for Accurate Gesture Classification
authors: Patil Vishal Ratansing; Pravin Game; Sagar Rane; Sagar G. Mohite; V. V. Sarbhukan; Yogesh Jadhav
venue: International journal of pattern recognition and artificial intelligence
abstract: Sign language recognition (SLR) plays a significant role in improving communication accessibility for hearing-impaired individuals, particularly in emergency scenarios where fast and reliable gesture interpretation is required. However, emergency Indian Sign Language (ISL) recognition remains challenging due to rapid hand movements, visually similar gestures, and complex spatial-temporal relationships among hand components. This study proposes an SLR-HIE-LKAGCN framework that integrates topology-aware spatial representation, spatial-temporal feature learning, graph-based gesture modeling, and optimization-based parameter adaptation for emergency ISL recognition. Initially, input gesture frames are processed using a Simplicial Convolutional Filter (SCF) to preserve higher-order spatial relationships among hand regions and enhance gesture representation. The refined gesture sequences are then provided to a Spatial-Temporal Knowledge-Embedded Transformer (STKET) to capture temporal dependencies and contextual movement patterns. The extracted features are further analyzed utilizing a Large-Kernel Attention Graph Convolutional Network (LKAGCN), which models relationships among hand landmarks and learns discriminative gesture representations. In addition, the Secretary Bird Optimization Algorithm (SBOA) is employed to optimize critical network parameters and improve model convergence. The proposed framework is evaluated on emergency ISL gesture categories, including accident, call, doctor, help, hot, lose, pain, and thief. Experimental outcomes establish that the proposed technique achieves superior recognition performance with 98.82% accuracy, 98.57% precision, and 98.53% F1-score, outperforming existing approaches. The obtained results indicate that SLR-HIE-LKAGCN provides an effective and computationally efficient solution for real-time emergency ISL recognition.

title: Openhands: A Skeleton-Based Graph Convolutional Framework for Large-Scale Sign Language Recognition and LLM-Driven Sign Language Generation
authors: Naman Chawla; Krishna Nagpal; Elakkiya Rajasekar; Angel Arul Jothi Joseph
venue: 2026 International Conference on Interactive Systems & Information Society Technologies (InterSys)
abstract: Automatic sign language recognition (SLR) remains a critical challenge in computer vision, with applications in accessibility and human-computer interaction. This paper presents OpenHands, a modular skeleton-based framework for wordlevel sign language recognition that leverages MediaPipe Holistic to extract skeletal keypoints, constructs spatio-temporal graphs representing signer motion, and classifies signs using a decoupled GCN architecture enhanced with Dense Pose Correspondence (DPC) self-supervised pretraining. We evaluate on WLASL1000 (1,000 classes, 21,083 videos) and AUTSL100 (100 classes, $\sim 3,000$ videos), achieving 83.2% Top-1 and 95.7% Top-5 accuracy on WLASL1000, and 88.1% Top-1 and 97.8% Top-5 accuracy on AUTSL100. The framework provides reusable dataset pipelines, configuration-driven experimentation, and comprehensive tooling for training, inference, and visualization, enabling rapid prototyping across multiple sign language corpora. Our results demonstrate that skeleton-based GCNs with self-supervised pretraining achieve competitive performance while maintaining computational efficiency and modularity. We further extend OpenHands with a sign language generation (SLG) module that employs a transformer decoder conditioned on large language model (LLM) text embeddings to synthesise temporally coherent skeletal keypoint sequences from natural language input, enabling bidirectional text-to-sign translation within a unified framework and achieving a back-translation BLEU of 17.8 on PHOENIX-2014T.

title: Multimodal Minimal-Angular-Geometry Representation for Real-Time Dynamic Mexican Sign Language Recognition
authors: Gerardo García-Gil; Gabriela del Carmen López-Armas; Yahir Emmanuel Ramirez-Pulido
venue: Technologies
abstract: Current approaches to dynamic sign language recognition commonly rely on dense landmark representations, which impose high computational cost and hinder real-time deployment on resource-constrained devices. To address this limitation, this work proposes a computationally efficient framework for real-time dynamic Mexican Sign Language (MSL) recognition based on a multimodal minimal angular-geometry representation. Instead of processing complete landmark sets (e.g., MediaPipe Holistic with up to 468 keypoints), the proposed method encodes the relational geometry of the hands, face, and upper body into a compact set of 28 invariant internal angular descriptors. This representation substantially reduces feature dimensionality and computational complexity while preserving linguistically relevant manual and non-manual information required for grammatical and semantic discrimination in MSL. A real-time end-to-end pipeline is developed, comprising multimodal landmark extraction, angular feature computation, and temporal modeling using a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network. The system is evaluated on a custom dataset of dynamic MSL gestures acquired under controlled real-time conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves 99% accuracy and 99% macro F1-score, matching state-of-the-art performance while using fewer features dramatically. The compactness, interpretability, and efficiency of the minimal angular descriptor make the proposed system suitable for real-time deployment on low-cost devices, contributing toward more accessible and inclusive sign language recognition technologies.

title: Multilingual signs recognition using recurrent neural network
authors: Thouseef Ulla Khan; Dileep Marichi Ramachandra
venue: IAES International Journal of Artificial Intelligence (IJ-AI)
abstract: Recognition of sign language is a crucial step towards providing individuals with hearing and speech impairment meaningful communication, but the fact that there are a number of distinct sign languages and gestures remain complex makes it a challenge to the current automated systems. The present paper describes a real-time multilingual sign language recognition system that is based on a recurrent neural network with long short-term memory (RNN-LSTM) with hand landmark MediaPipe-based hand landmark detection to successfully receive spatial and temporal gesture features. The proposed system was trained and tested over a self-collected set of alphabet gestures of the Chinese, American, and Indian sign language, including one hand and two-hand gestures, and was run with Keras with extensive performance evaluation metrics. The strength and generalization abilities of the suggested approach as part of different gesture patterns and variations in users are confirmed by experimental outcomes that indicate high recognition rates of 99.58%, 99.62%, and 99.63% of the Chinese, American, and Indian sign languages, respectively. These results demonstrate the promise of the given framework as a dedicated assistive system of communication and give it a solid base to continue its development to the point of the system of the continuous sign language recognition (CSLR) and multimodal translators.

title: Multi-view Integration with View-specific Self-attention for Sign Language Recognition
authors: Q. H. Hoang; Anh Vu Tran
venue: Journal of Image and Graphics
abstract: — Sign Language Recognition (SLR) plays a pivotal role in mitigating communication barriers between the deaf community and broader society. Recently, the Video Transformer Network (VTN), an extension of the transformer architecture incorporating a multi-head self-attention mechanism, has demonstrated efficacy in video processing tasks and SLR. However, relying solely on Red Green Blue (RGB) frame information may render the model susceptible to redundant data and environmental factors such as lighting variations and complex backgrounds. Additionally, most existing SLR datasets provide only frontal viewpoints, which constrain the model ’ s generalizability, particularly in real-world settings where diverse perspectives are prevalent. In this study, we propose Video Transformer Network with 3 Graph Convolutional Network (VTN3GCN), a multi-view and multi-stream framework that integrates RGB data, skeleton coordinates, and pose flow from three distinct viewpoints: left, right, and center. This architecture enhances VTN by incorporating Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) to learn skeletal frame features and employs an early fusion mechanism between the RGB and skeleton streams. Experiments conducted on the Multi-VSL200 dataset — a newly curated dataset for Vietnamese Sign Language (VSL) featuring three viewpoints per video demonstrate that the VTN3GCN framework achieves a top-1 accuracy of up to 92.92%, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/fossbk/MultiView-ISLR/tree/main/VTN3 GCN.

title: Multi-Modal Indian Sign Language Translation based on Hand-Face Landmark Fusion with Grammar-Aware Sentence Generation
authors: V. R.; C. Chethan; Sreenivas Madupu; Sravanthi Dama; M. Dileep; P. Sathish
venue: 2026 International Conference on Next-Gen Intelligent Computing and Applications (ICONICA)
abstract: Individuals with hearing difficulties always find it hard to communicate to the outside world. Generating meaningful English text and speech using automated tools is helpful for them. This study presents a multi-modal system to address such problems. The system translates Indian Sign Language to a grammar-aware texts and speeches. The proposed system integrates hand gesture recognition, facial expression analysis, and speech processing. The method initially extracts visual and audio features from webcam and microphone inputs, then performs multi-modal feature fusion. The system uses a lightweight deep learning model, to improve fluency and contextual accuracy by applying grammar-aware language processing. The study reduces transient recognition errors using a stability filtering mechanism. This in turn enhances prediction consistency by delivering text and synthesized speech as output. The study provides an accessible and interactive communication platform and improves translation naturalness. By combining multi-modal perception with linguistic refinement, the study makes it suitable for real-time assistive communication applications.

title: Multi-Modal Feature Integration for Comprehensive SIBI Sign Language Translation
authors: I Dewa Made Bayu Atmaja Darmawan; Linawati Linawati; Gede Sukadarmika; Ni Made Ary Esta Dewi Wirastuti; Reza Pulungan
venue: JOIV: International Journal on Informatics Visualization
matched_terms: sign language recognition, sign language translation, signer-independent
abstract: This study uses a multi-stage approach to extract information from sign gesture videos in the sign language translation (SLT) process. Sign recognition is performed using features from both manual components (hand gestures) and non-manual components, such as facial expressions and lip movements. The combination of these two components is expected to increase the semantic depth and accuracy of the Indonesian Sign Language System (SIBI) video translation results. The proposed framework includes word-level video segmentation, frame reduction (frame selection), facial expression recognition (FER), sign language recognition (Sign2Gloss), and sign language translation (Gloss2Text). This study proposes an optical flow-based approach for word segmentation and frame selection, called Motion-Adaptive Frame Selection Optical Flow-Based (MAFS-OF). MAFS-OF selects frames by examining significant differences between adjacent frames as signs of movement. This study presents the test results in detail at each stage. In the expression recognition stage, the VGG7-MP-32 architecture combined with ConvLSTM obtained the best F1-score of 0.866. Furthermore, during the Sign2Gloss stage, the ConvLSTM architecture outperformed STMC. However, STMC displayed more stable values in signer-independent testing. In the final stage, this study used the T5 model to translate the set of glosses generated in the Sign2Gloss stage and the emotions generated in the FER stage. Tests using BLEU, ROUGH-L, and METEOR showed strong consistency in generating new sentences from glosses and emotions. This study proves that the proposed framework can effectively translate sign language by combining manual and non-manual components for signer-dependent scenarios. Efforts to improve generalization for sign-independent signing remain a challenge that requires further refinement.

title: Multi-Modal Assistive Communication System: Real-Time American Sign Language Recognition, Lip Reading, and Morse code Translation Using Browser-Based AI
authors: V. Laxmi
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
abstract: Communication barriers significantly impede social participation for the estimated 466 million individuals worldwide with disabling hearing loss and the additional millions affected by speech and motor impairments. Existing assistive technologies are characterised by three persistent deficiencies: single-modality coverage that obliges users to manage multiple fragmented tools, dependence on cloud-based inference that compromises user privacy, and prohibitive acquisition costs that restrict access in low-resource settings. This paper presents the Multi-Modal Assistive Communication System (MMACS), a unified browserbased artificial intelligence platform that simultaneously addresses all three deficiencies. MMACS integrates American Sign Language (ASL) gesture recognition (30 signs, ~10–15% of the full lexicon), AI-driven lip reading through viseme detection, and interactive Morse code translation within a single web application requiring no software installation. The system employs MediaPipe for real-time hand and facial landmark detection, TensorFlow.js for client-side neural network inference, and the Web Speech API for voice synthesis — all executing locally on the user's device to ensure data privacy. Empirical evaluation with 50 participants (18 with hearing impairments, 12 with speech impairments, 8 with motor impairments, 12 neurotypical controls) demonstrated ASL recognition accuracy of 94.2% (±2.1%), lip reading accuracy of 87.8% (±3.4%), and sub-200 ms end-to-end latency across all modalities. The mobile-first responsive architecture ensures compatibility across all major browser engines on desktop, tablet, and mobile form factors. A post-study satisfaction survey recorded a 92% positive rating, indicating strong perceived utility in controlled settings. MMACS establishes a reproducible, open-source benchmark for privacy-preserving assistive communication technology and furnishes a principled framework for future multi-modal human-computer interaction research.

title: MAG-KD: Mask-Guided Adaptive Gating Knowledge Distillation for Skeleton-Based Sign Language Recognition on Edge Devices
authors: Dao Tuan Dat Vo; V. Nguyen; T. Nguyen; Minh Huan Vo
venue: IEEE Access
abstract: While artificial intelligence has significantly advanced sign language recognition (SLR), high-performing models often entail substantial computational complexity. This creates a significant barrier to deploying real-time applications on resource-constrained edge hardware. While knowledge distillation (KD) offers a potential solution, existing multi-teacher strategies are predominantly tailored for static images and remain unoptimized for skeleton-based graph convolutional networks (GCNs), which are inherently sensitive to pose estimation noise and require modeling complex temporal-semantic dependencies. To address this, we propose Mask-Guided Adaptive Gating Knowledge Distillation (MAG-KD), a framework specifically tailored for skeleton-based GCNs. Our approach adopts a decoupled distillation strategy, integrating a Mask-Guided Filtering Mechanism based on correctness-aware principles to strictly filter noisy supervision, and an Adaptive Gating Network leveraging context-aware features to dynamically synthesize teacher knowledge based on input complexity. Extensive evaluations across multiple random seeds demonstrate the superior stability of our approach. On the AUTSL dataset, our lightweight MAG-KD student (Student-M, 0.48M parameters) achieves a highly robust Top-1 mean accuracy of 94.25% $\pm ~0.19$ . Furthermore, our method proves strong cross-dataset generalization by achieving 66.33% $\pm ~0.54$ on the WLASL-100 subset, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art KD methods. Comprehensive hardware profiling on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano confirms optimal edge feasibility: the deployed model achieves a real-time inference speed of 33.13 frames per second (FPS) while maintaining a highly efficient power profile of merely 6.23 W. Extended analysis indicates that the proposed algorithm operates optimally within the standard edge model regime, whereas static ensemble strategies remain more effective for ultra-compressed architectures with fewer than 100K parameters.

title: MACHINE LEARNING MODEL FOR RECOGNITION OF UKRAINIAN SIGN LANGUAGE HAND CONFIGURATIONS
authors: N. Nedashkovskaya; Kostiantyn Grishyn
venue: KPI Science News
abstract: Background. Sign language recognition using Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a relevant and still unsolved problem. For Ukrainian Sign Language (USL), the task is complicated by a lack of publicly available datasets. Consequently, researchers operating under data-constrained conditions should apply additional features for improving model accuracy. Hand configuration is a fundamental characteristic of lexical units in any sign language. In USL 40 configurations exist. The ability to accurately identify configuration would provide relevant features for AI-based sign language recognition systems. Objective. To develop a machine learning model capable of frame-by-frame recognition of USL hand configurations on a video stream with an accuracy of at least 95% on the test set and an average inference time not exceeding 70 ms. Methods. As input data for the USL hand configurations recognition models, a system of mathematical indicators, calculated from the keypoints coordinates, extracted via MediaPipe pose estimation system, was proposed. The training dataset was created from camera images of USL hand configurations performed by middle-aged subjects. Following keypoints extraction through MediaPipe, the corresponding vectors of mathematical indicators were computed. Various architectures of random forest and perceptron were evaluated. Results. The highest performance was achieved by the perceptron with two hidden layers of 300 neurons each, which takes the vector of proposed mathematical indicators as input. The model reached an accuracy of 98.18% on the test set. During testing on a video stream, it identified without error 32 out of 40 USL configurations, and with only sporadic deviations. The average inference latency was 46 ms. Notably, a perceptron of identical architecture trained on raw MediaPipe keypoint coordinates exhibited lower accuracy on a video stream. Furthermore, the proposed indicators improved random forest model performance, confirming their universality. Conclusion. The optimal model among the considered architectures was a perceptron with two hidden layers of 300 neurons each, which takes the vector of proposed mathematical indicators as input. It identifies in real-time USL hand configurations, achieving an accuracy of 98.18% on the test set. In experiments based on the proposed expert assessment criterion on the video stream, it correctly identified 35% more configurations (80% vs. 45%), compared to the model based on raw keypoint coordinates. Therefore, implementing additional verification based on expert assessment in addition to the standard accuracy metric on the test data is effective. The presented architecture is the first artificial intelligence-based model for the USL hand configuration recognition. Future research will focus on integrating this network into a system for isolated recognition of USL.

title: Low-Complexity Sign Language Recognition: A Cross-Modal Distillation Approach for State-Space Models
authors: Victor Costa; Lucas Superti; Brenda Salenave Santana; Tatiana Bolívar Lebedeff; Guilherme Corrêa
venue: Brazilian Symposium on Multimedia and the Web
matched_terms: sign language recognition, sign language translation, landmark, signer-independent
abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) is a fundamental challenge for digital accessibility and interactive multimedia systems. While state-of-the-art approaches that rely on 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (e.g., I3D) achieve high accuracy by extracting dense spatiotemporal features directly from RGB videos, their high computational cost makes them prohibitive for real-time edge computing applications. Conversely, lightweight models based on spatial landmarks significantly reduce computational overhead but suffer from a severe drop in accuracy due to the loss of implicit visual semantic context, such as subtle hand depths and environmental textures. To address the dichotomy between computational efficiency and semantic richness, this paper proposes a Cross-Modal Knowledge Distillation pipeline for Brazilian Sign Language (LIBRAS) recognition. We utilize an I3D network operating on raw video as the Teacher model to transfer "soft probabilities" to a Mamba 1D Student model operating exclusively on spatial coordinates extracted via MediaPipe. Experimental results demonstrate that our cross-modal distillation approach successfully bridges the semantic gap. While a vanilla Mamba 1D model (trained without distillation) achieves only 71% signer-independent accuracy, our proposed distilled approach elevates this performance to 78%. Remarkably, this 7% absolute improvement introduces zero computational overhead during inference. The proposed distilled Mamba 1D model achieves real-time latency (0.21 ms), requires only 9.81 MB of VRAM, and consumes a mere 0.004 Joules per inference, representing a 99.7% reduction in energy consumption compared to the video-based baseline. These results demonstrate the viability of deploying highly accurate, semantically aware sign language translation systems natively on resource-constrained mobile and IoT devices.

title: Lightweight Kinematic Feature Representation for Word-Level Bangla Sign Language Recognition
authors: Aseer Muntaqueem Ferdous Arko; Ishrat Shabnam; K. Halder
venue: 2026 International Conference on Power, Electronics, Communications, Computing, and Intelligent Infrastructure (PECCII)
abstract: Existing sign language recognition systems often focus on letter-level recognition through spatial data extracted from static images or rely on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) operating directly on pixel-level video data, which can be computationally expensive and can limit scalability and real-time applicability. This work attempts to establish a lightweight, efficient, feature-based framework for the recognition of dynamic gestures from Bangla sign language. This framework is used on the BdSLW60 Bangla sign word gesture video dataset, consisting of 9307 videos in 60 classes. Each video frame is encoded using an 86-dimensional kinematic feature vector per hand derived from the normalized hand landmarks extracted using MediaPipe Hands, finger articulation angles, wrist orientation, and bounding box geometry. Then, velocity features are modeled through temporal derivatives. Experimental results show high efficacy across multiple architectures. Scalability analysis shows that while accuracy decreases as vocabulary grows from 15 to 60 classes, the models remain robust; under random splitting, the Random Forest (RF), CNN, Transformer, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) classifiers achieved accuracies of 98.5%, 98.7%, 97.9%, and 98.5%, respectively, for 15 classes and 96%, 96.5%, 96.9%, and 94.8%, respectively, for 60 classes. In signer-independent holdout tests, the RF classifier outperformed others with 85.5% accuracy for 15 classes. These findings prove the framework’s potential as a lightweight solution.

title: Lightweight Hand Gesture Recognition for Sign Language Using MediaPipe and CNN-LSTM
authors: K. Kumar; V. S. Rani
venue: 2026 5th OPJU International Technology Conference (OTCON) on Smart Computing for Innovation and Advancement in Industry 5.0
abstract: Recognizing hand gestures is essential for Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Assistive Communication Systems, particularly for deaf and speech-impaired individuals. Although recent gesture recognition techniques achieve strong performance, most rely on computationally expensive CNN or 3D-CNN architectures, require dedicated GPU acceleration, or use costly sensing hardware, which restricts real-world deployment. This paper proposes a lightweight and deployable hybrid Sign Language Recognition (SLR) framework that integrates MediaPipe hand landmark extraction with a CNN classifier for static gestures and a CNN-LSTM classifier for dynamic gestures, optimized using post-training quantization for edge deployment. Static gestures trained on the ASL-MNIST dataset achieve 98.5% accuracy using a compact CNN model, while dynamic gestures involving 25 ASL words trained from MediaPipe-generated temporal sequences achieve 93.7% accuracy using a CNN-LSTM network. Model compression reduces the static and dynamic model sizes to 4.9 MB and 12.1 MB, respectively—2× to 10× smaller than comparable state-of-the-art methods-while retaining competitive performance. The proposed models are implemented in real time on CPU-only systems and achieve approximately 80 FPS for static gestures and 35 FPS for dynamic gestures in a Flask-based system. Compared with recent studies, the proposed hybrid solution offers one of the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and is suitable for scalable assistive communication systems.

title: Lightweight CNN and Grad-CAM Integration for Interpreting Arabic Sign Language Hijaiyyah Letter Classification
authors: Akbar Sidqi; A. Rizkiya
venue: Jurnal Komputer dan Elektro Sains
abstract: Communication plays an important role in social life as a means of conveying information and building interactions between humans. For individuals who are deaf and mute, sign language serves as a visual communication medium that supports the process of conveying messages. One of the sign language systems is Arabic Sign Language (ArSL), which utilises the Hijaiyyah letters through the fingerspelling method to spell out certain terms or vocabulary. However, the limited understanding of sign language within society still poses a barrier to social interaction. This research develops an Arabic Sign Language (ArSL) Hijaiyyah letter classification system based on a Lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with the aim of producing a model that has high performance and low computational requirements. Additionally, the Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) method using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is applied to enhance the transparency of classification results through the visualisation of important areas in the images. Based on the test results, the developed model achieved an accuracy of 0.84, a precision of 0.84, a recall of 0.84, an F1-score of 0.84 and a an Specificity of 0.99. The Grad-CAM visualisation results show that the model focuses on the relevant hand areas during the prediction process. The findings of this study indicate that the system is capable of performing classification with good and measurable performance, as well as supporting real-time sign language recognition with a short response time, thereby improving communication accessibility for individuals with disabilities.

title: Lightweight Bidirectional Sign Language Translation for Inclusive Education on Edge Devices
authors: Youssef Amzoug; Chaimae Elfakir; Khadija Hicham; Soufiane Hamida; S. Ziti; B. Cherradi
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Innovative Research in Applied Science, Engineering and Technology (IRASET)
abstract: (Providing equitable and high-quality education to Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHH) students is the main principle of the modern pedagogical framework, and the practical implementation of this principle is often hindered by the prohibitive cost and delays of the manual interpretation. This paper proposes a two-way, AI-based sign-language translation system, which has been carefully selected to be run on resource-constrained edge computing platforms in real-time. It is bifurcated into two main pipelines: first, a Sign-to-Text (S2T) module which combines the MediaPipe skeletal landmarks with a small one-dimensional (1D)CNN, and second, a Speech-to-Sign (STS) module with an offline Mozilla-DeepSpeech automatic speech recognition (ASR) and Blender-based three-dimensional (3D) animations. The framework, where this architecture is implemented in the form of a Moodle Learning Management System (LMS) plugin using WebSockets, achieves classification results up to 97.0 percent and a total end-toend latency of only 185 ms on general central-processing-unit (CPU) hardware. Importantly, converting high-resolution video input to a brief 63-coordinate skeletal vector output not only provides student privacy protection, but also avoids the use of a high-end graphics processing unit (GPU) acceleration that has made scalable inclusive educational implementations achievable.)

title: Landmark-Driven Real-Time American Sign Language Recognition via CNN–BiLSTM Fusion on Mobile Platforms
authors: G. S; H. E; Quba Jaslin C; Kiruba Wesley ap
venue: 2026 International Conference on Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision (ICNPCV)
abstract: Bridging the communication gap between deaf and hard of hearing individuals and the hearing community remains a significant challenge in areas such as healthcare, education, workplaces, and daily social interactions. American Sign Language (ASL) serves as a primary mode of communication for many deaf individuals; however, the limited availability of qualified sign language interpreters often restricts effective communication. This paper proposes a lightweight, real-time ASL recognition system based on a hybrid CNN-BiLSTM architecture optimized for mobile platforms. The proposed framework employs MediaPipe Hands to extract 21 hand landmarks from each frame, significantly reducing computational complexity while preserving essential gesture information. Spatial features are learned using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), while temporal dependencies between gesture sequences are captured using a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network. The model is trained on large scale ASL datasets and optimized using TensorFlow Lite for efficient on-device inference. Experimental results demonstrate a 95.2% recognition accuracy on the WLASL2000 dataset while maintaining real-time performance at 62 frames per second with a compact 8 MB model size. The proposed system enables accurate, fast, and accessible sign language recognition on smartphones without requiring specialized hardware or continuous internet connectivity, making it a practical assistive solution for real-world communication.

title: LLM-Powered Real-Time Sign Language Recognition and Translation using OpenCV and MediaPipe
authors: Mouna G. S.; H. M; Anil Kumar Reddy M; M. B; Shyam Sundar V
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Expert Clouds and Applications (ICOECA)
abstract: This paper introduces HandTalk, a real-time system for recognizing sign language and translating multiple languages, aimed at bridging communication gaps between hearing individuals and those who are deaf or hard of hearing.
